Response to Reviewers – Fredborg, Clark, & Smith

We would like to thank the three reviewers for their thorough critiques of our original submission.  In order to demonstrate that we have addressed each concern, we will discuss each point in order, starting with Reviewer 1.

Reviewer 1 (Anonymous) 
Validity of the findings 
Several issues have been identified:1. The recruitment of the controls is straightforward; however, it isn’t clear how it was established that the participants in the ASMR group did indeed experience ASMR. The authors mention they were recruited from ASMR Reddit site, however, raw data set and the supplemental materials do not seem to include any methods of verification of ASMR. Were they asked explicitly whether they experience ASMR (as were the controls)? There are questions related to how often they watch ASMR videos etc. on the ASMR checklist but many people enjoy watching such videos without experiencing the sensory response. Therefore, I am concerned that as these participants didn’t explicitly state that they experience the physiological response which constitutes ASMR, there is no way of knowing whether they indeed experience ASMR.
Response: Reviewer 1 is correct in noting that we did not ask ASMR participants to view a video to confirm their ASMR status.  This was intentional.  We were concerned that eliciting ASMR tingles prior to the completion of the study could potentially bias the results.  Several items on our questionnaires (in the current study and in Fredborg et al., 2017) related to emotional states.  Inducing ASMR, which is emotionally positive in nature, may have altered participants’ results.  Additionally, having one group of participants experiencing ASMR tingles while the other group (controls) would have introduced an inherent bias into the experimental design.  
We should note, however, that if an individual did not experience ASMR, then he or she would not have indicated experiencing tingles in response to any of the ASMR triggers listed in the ASMR Checklist.  The fact that all participants identified specific ASMR triggers (and the speed with which they elicited tingling sensations) suggests that our ASMR participants did, in fact, have ASMR.
That said, after reading Reviewer 1’s comments, we agree that it would be useful to more clearly explain how we were able to ensure that the ASMR participants experienced ASMR.  To that end, we have added the following statement to the Participants section, “To gain confidence that individuals recruited to the ASMR group genuinely experienced the phenomenon (rather than watched the videos for relaxation purposes), they were asked to answer specific questions about their ASMR experiences when completing a self-created ASMR checklist (Fredborg et al., 2017; as elaborated below). These questions included a list of 14 popular ASMR-triggering stimuli that participants rated both on the intensity of tingling sensations experienced, as well as how many seconds after stimulus onset that they would typically experience tingles. Only participants who completed the entirety of the ASMR checklist were included in the ASMR group during the analyses.”
2. The raw data set doesn’t include answers to all questions listed in ASMR checklist. E.g. this question is missing: ‘What is the earliest age you can recall having an ASMR experience? (For example, if you remember first having an ASMR experience at the age of four, please choose "4". In this question, a "first ASMR experience" refers to the first time that you noticed you were experiencing ASMR-related tingles, even if at the time you did not know what they were called’).
Response: We thank the reviewer for noting these omissions.  We initially did not include them because they are not discussed in the manuscript. They have been added to an updated data file.

3. Means and SDs should either be stated in the results section or a reference to the table containing this information should be provided. 

Response: A table of the means and SDs has been previously reported in our publication in Frontiers in Psychology (Table 2, Page 5): Fredborg, B., Clark, J., & Smith, S.D. (2017). An examination of personality traits associated with autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR). Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 247. doi: 10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00247. This description was added to our manuscript.

6. The explanation of the gender differences on Curiosity subscale of the TMS is a bit vague. Could the authors elaborate on what is meant by ‘attentional mechanisms’ and ‘more cognitive processes’ (p.15, line 349)?

7. I don’t think that consistency of ASMR tingles to specific triggers has been examined and established so far. Therefore, it is probably better to not include this description (p.2 line 43) 
Response: We thank the reviewer for this well-taken point. We have updated this sentence in the manuscript by replacing the word “consistently” with “frequently”.  Based on our conversations with participants and on our reading of online forums dedicated to ASMR, we believe that “frequently” is an accurate term to use in this instance.


Reviewer 2 (Marisa del Campo) 
Basic reporting 
The writing is excellent technically and easy to follow, with very clear and precise wording. As a whole, the article is tight and flows well. The literature review is concise, yet provides a solid explanation of ASMR, its relationship to mindfulness, and the rationale for the investigation. The references are relevant. It may be worthwhile to consider expanding the background to include previous findings regarding other traits associated with ASMR (e.g., Fredborg, Clark & Smith, 2016; Janik McErlean & Banissy, 2017). I think it is up to the authors' discretion, however, whether it would fit into the nicely focused structure of this article. Results are clearly reported, and the use of headings to separate results by instrument makes for a straightforward reading experience. The raw data has been shared as requested, along with consent form and human subjects approval. 
Response: We thank Reviewer 2 for her positive comments on our article.  The reviewer is correct in noting that we did not allocate much space to a discussion of our earlier results (Fredborg et al., 2017), as we wanted to keep the structure of our introduction focused on mindfulness and ASMR.  That said, we have now added information about Janik and colleagues’ (2017) paper to our Introduction.  
Experimental design 
This is a methodologically sound research article on a topic relevant to the health sciences. The authors present a defined research question and state their hypotheses. The aim of the study is to offer "novel insight into the phenomenology of ASMR, while also showing how this atypical conscious state is related to mindful states and traits." Recruitment methods and all procedures are clearly indicated. The instruments are well-described with technical properties reported. The inclusion of the author-designed ASMR Checklist in the supplemental materials also allows for replicability of results. 
Response: We are again grateful to Reviewer 2 for her positive comments on our article.  
Validity of the findings 
The authors used age and sex-matched participants and utilized an additional screening method for ASMR to ensure the samples were accurately represented. I did wonder about the potential for sampling bias because different methods were used to recruit ASMR and non-ASMR participants, and perhaps this should be noted. Results are reported with specificity, including both significant and non-significant findings. I appreciated that authors often noted the strength of correlations presented. They justifiably conclude that there appears to be a correlation between mindfulness and ASMR, as is supported by the findings of this research. They raise a number of interesting questions (e.g., whether ASMR is a cognitively active process) and potential future research directions (e.g., whether mindfulness training would increase likelihood of ASMR).
Response: We thank the reviewer for these thoughtful comments. We added a brief note in the Methods and Materials section to elaborate that individuals with ASMR recruited from Reddit and control participants recruited from Qualtrics are both recruited from samples of users that are likely regular internet users: “Age- and sex-matched control participants were recruited by the participant recruitment team at Qualtrics Panels (Qualtrics, Inc., Provo, UT) which is an internet-based participant recruitment company. Using this recruitment method allowed us to mitigate sampling bias by increasing the likelihood that both ASMR and control participants were regular internet users.”
Reviewer 3 (James Heathers) 
Comments for the Author 
This study is on an extremely interesting phenomenon, and one which is chronically under-investigated compared to its popular interest. The authors should be commended for their understanding and approach of such a topic, which might be regarded as falling outside the range of 'acceptable' topics for an academic endeavour.As the field is nascent, I feel it is appropriate for review to be reasonably forgiving - all preliminary work such as this is eventually at the very least heavily qualified by later replications and more concrete concepts. To try to hold the work to a standard of a well-established field may serve to not allow the field to develop at all. However, it also pays to be scrupulous.
Response: We agree wholeheartedly with the reviewer and appreciate his being meticulous in reviewing this manuscript.
These are points as they occur in order. I have left page numbers in the copied sections for reference:* "In addition, the intensity and duration of ASMR57 experiences are often under the control of the individual, a characteristic that distinguishes58 ASMR from the automatic sensory responses of synesthesia."It is a shame this point was not expanded further. As far as I am aware, synesthesia is an entirely automatic and non-conscious mechanism. However, ASMR is - presumably - capable of being suppressed even when participants encounter a strong stimulus. This is a strong piece of evidence in favour of the similarity to mindfulness (especially when experienced as a cultivated habit or meditation). Future work would do well to include an item about the *capability of suppressing ASMR*, which may vary with the perceived strength of the phenomenon.Response: We agree with the reviewer that the capability of suppressing ASMR is an area of interest in future work. In fact, we added items about the ability to suppress ASMR to an online study that we just completed (data analysis is still underway).  We were a bit hesitant to expand upon this point in our original submission, as the idea had been discussed in previous ASMR publications (e.g., Fredborg et al., 2017; del Campo & Kehle, 2016).  We also still do not know if everyone with ASMR has this ability or if it is only present in a subpopulation of individuals with ASMR.  Given this uncertainty, we decided to keep our introduction focused as much as possible on ASMR and mindfulness.  That said, we sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion and have added a line about the capability of suppressing ASMR in the Introduction section: “In addition, the intensity and duration of ASMR experiences are often under the control of the individual, a characteristic that distinguishes ASMR from the automatic sensory responses of synesthesia. Indeed, the ability to suppress ASMR responses as they arise may be an important aspect of this phenomenon that warrants further study”.
* "A principal-components analysis of the 14 items on the checklist revealed five “intensity” factors underlying the common ASMR-triggering stimuli chosen for the checklist, each of which had an eigenvalue greater than 1.0. These intensity factors (with items in parentheses) were Watching (“Watching others paint,” “Watching others draw,” “Watching others open a package,” and “Watching others cook”), Touching (“Watching someone touch another person’s hair,” “Watching someone touch their own hair,” “Watching others apply makeup and/or nail polish to themselves,” and “Watching others apply makeup and/or nail polish to another person”), Repetitive Sounds (“Tapping sounds” and “Scratching sounds”), Simulations (“Dentist simulation” and “Haircut simulation”), and Mouth Sounds (“Chewing sounds” and“Whispering”), respectively (Fredborg et al., 2017)."Consider reducing this to a Table?
Response: We agree with the reviewer that this sentence contains a great deal of information.  However, after rewriting the sentence (multiple times) to explain the five ASMR trigger types (e.g., Watching others), we found that the sentence was only marginally shorter than the original while also requiring the addition of a new table.  So, our attempted solution would use up more space in the journal than our original sentence (while not improving clarity).  We therefore opted to keep our original wording.  * Where were Control individuals recruited?
Response: Control participants were recruited through Qualtrics Panels (similar to MTurk).  This information is found in the following sentence in the Participants section: “Age- and sex-matched control participants were recruited by the participant recruitment team at Qualtrics Panels (Qualtrics, Inc., Provo, UT) which is an internet-based participant recruitment company.”* "112 The current study received ethical approval from the Department of Psychology’s Human113 Research Ethics Committee (HREB)."  Is this a typo?
Response: We thank the reviewer for noting this confusing acronym. We changed this wording to reflect that it is the University of Winnipeg’s Human Research Ethics Board.
* Explicitly state (a) this is an exploratory study, and require ongoing verification (b) it is speculative to conduct a power analysis with entirely novel questions, so one was not conducted.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have included this note in our manuscript in the Methods and Materials section: “Given the exploratory nature of this study, an a priori power analysis to determine the ideal sample size for a given effect size would have been based on speculation and was thus not conducted”.
* The correlation between Tcur and MAAS is reported for the whole sample, however, it appears from the subsamples that the relationship in ASMR participants (r=0.13) is substantially lower than for the regular sample (r=0.27).
Response: We thank the reviewer for catching this oversight. We edited table 2 such that the r value reflects ASMR participants only. We also edited the text such that these differences are made clear.
* Is the Embodied Emotion scale absent? It appears in the study description, but neither the data set nor the results. 
Response: The Embodied Emotion Scale (EES) was included in this study as part of a multi-study attempt to validate this new measure.  Thus far, we have conducted psychometric testing and have used EES scores as covariates in a resting-state fMRI study examining individual differences in the functional connectivity of several resting-state networks.  We were hoping to show that the EES also differentiated groups that were prone to high degrees of embodiment (ASMR) from control participants.  As these data will (hopefully) be used in a different publication, we did not list them here and did not include these data in the attached dataset.  However, as the reviewer is interested, here is a summary of the Results for this measure.  All comparisons between ASMR and Control participants were statistically significant (except anger, which would not be significant when the p-value is corrected for multiple comparisons).

* Qualtrix returns forms which only allow continuation between screens until answers are complete. However, the raw data is missing from an estimated 40 to 60 cells. Was this lost before or after collection? Include an explicit statement of adjusted n's for each calculation.
Response: Missing values represent values that were not filled in by participants completing the study (i.e., were lost during data collection). Only participants who completed all questionnaire items, identified as either male or female (for sex-matching purposes), and who did not write any post-study comments indicating that they had intentionally distorted their responses were included in the study analyses (N = 173 ASMR participants with scores for all checklist items, MAAS items, and TMS – Curiosity items.)
* On Table 1, what does ASMR (M) denote?
Response: We thank the reviewer for catching this typing error (“(M)” from table 1). The (M) represented the mean score for individuals with ASMR; however, is already described in the text above the table and was removed for clarity.* The first participant in the questionnaire in the ASMR group does not appear to show any symptoms of ASMR in response to any trigger. Was this a test line left in by accident?
Response: We apologize for the confusion. All participants’ data were left in the dataset to be as transparent as possible. This participant would have been removed from the analyses due to their lack of responses on the questionnaire.
* Also in this data, the averages in column BE do not match the columns AK through AX. Is this because some of the items were redacted? The items are reported as 14, however they are numbered to 16, and several "optional" items were apparently measured but not included. Please clarify.
Response: Again, our apologies for this confusion. Sixteen stimuli items were initially included in the ASMR checklist, however, two of these were removed because a very small proportion of the sample reported familiarity with these items (“watching others sweep” and “watching others refill fountain pens”). As such, we were left with 14 popular ASMR-inducing stimuli to be analyzed. This process was detailed in our initial manuscript using the ASMR checklist (see Fredborg et al., 2017). The following text was added to the Materials and Methods section for clarification: “After initial analyses (as described in Fredborg et al., 2017), two of these 16 items were removed because only a very small proportion of the sample reported familiarity with these items. These stimuli items were “watching others sweep” and “watching others refill fountain pens”. As such, 14 popular ASMR-inducing stimuli were analyzed.” Moreover, optional items were not analyzed, as they were qualitative and thus all differed between participants. A future manuscript could analyze these responses. 
* I cannot reconcile the "STIM" values in the spreadsheets being null for participants when all the other data is given. This may be my misunderstanding. 
Response: Individuals with any missing stimuli intensity rating values, or with a value of “7” (“unknown”) were not scored on the factor loadings.

We hope that our detailed responses to the reviewers’ queries have addressed any concerns that they had with our manuscript.  We thank the reviewers once again for their thorough critiques of our original submission.
